title_original: The Weight of Things: The Hidden Lives of Everyday Materials
excerpt_original: At the Iziko South African National Gallery, ‘Matereality V2’ explores how contemporary artists across Africa transform everyday materials into powerful expressions of memory, identity, labour and belonging. 13 october 2025 What happens when the materials […]

blocks.text: At the Iziko South African National Gallery, ‘Matereality V2’ explores how contemporary artists across Africa transform everyday materials into powerful expressions of memory, identity, labour and belonging.

What happens when the materials we overlook become the very substance of artistic meaning? In ‘Materiality V2’, curator Andrea Lewis brings together emerging and established artists whose practices challenge conventional distinctions between art, craft and everyday life. From textiles and found objects to industrial waste and organic matter, the exhibition reveals how materials carry histories of extraction, cultural knowledge, human experience and transformation.

In conversation with ART AFRICA, Lewis reflects on the evolving relationship between material and meaning, the importance of physical making in an increasingly digital world, and museums’ role in reconsidering what we preserve, value, and remember. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

blocks.caption: Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

blocks.text: Suzette Bell-Roberts: The title ‘Matereality V2’ brings together material and reality. In this exhibition, what does “matereality” mean, and how has that idea evolved in this second iteration?

Andrea Lewis: For me, matereality is the point at which material and lived reality become inseparable. Materials are never neutral: they arrive with histories, associations, labour, politics, memory and social realities already attached to them. A blanket means something before it becomes an artwork. Hair means something. Soil means something. A cement bag, clothing, plastic, beads, soap or electronic waste all carry social and cultural associations. Artists activate those histories. These materials are not simply unusual substitutes for paint, bronze or marble; their meanings are inseparable from the meanings of the works themselves. The material is not decoration around the idea. It is part of the idea.

The first ‘Matereality’ developed out of something I had been noticing at ISANG: artists were increasingly moving beyond traditional media in ways that challenged the categories museums rely upon. Paintings incorporated rubber, hair, engine oil, textiles and found objects. Sculpture drew from craft, industry, clothing and performance. The distinctions between painting, sculpture, textiles, installation and works on paper were becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. That exhibition included artists who were already very well known, including Igshaan Adams and Usha Seejarim, alongside many others experimenting deliberately with unconventional materials. And then COVID happened. The exhibition opened in 2020 and almost immediately entered this strange period in which museums and galleries were closing. But the idea stayed with me.

Six years later, the context has shifted again. We are living through extraordinary digital acceleration and the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, while many artists are investing enormous amounts of time in intensely physical processes: stitching, weaving, cutting, binding, layering, assembling and repeating. I do not necessarily see this as a rejection of technology, but physical making feels more significant in an increasingly dematerialised world. Materials have weight, texture, resistance and physical presence. So ‘Matereality V2’ gives us insight into the realities of individual artists, but also into the state of the world around us. Through material, it opens onto questions of land and belonging, labour and the body, memory and family, indigenous knowledge, colonial histories, consumption and waste, environmental concerns, and value. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

blocks.text: How were the artists and works for ‘Matereality V2’ selected , and what conversations emerged among their different practices?

The selection process began while the first ‘Matereality’ was still on exhibition. I started writing down the names of artists I wished I had known about, or had been able to include, the first time around – artists such as Sepideh Mehraban, Gaelen Pinnock and Promise Mapondera. That list stayed pinned to my wall for the next six years. Whenever I encountered a work that made me think differently about material, I would add the artist’s name. Sometimes that happened in an exhibition, during a studio visit, at an art fair, in the news, or even on Instagram. I would then do a deeper dive into the artist’s practice and, wherever possible, visit their studio and speak to them. Sometimes an artist also made something specifically with this exhibition in mind.

Eventually the list grew to around 150 artists, so the difficulty was not finding enough work. It was deciding what to leave out. There are many artists I would dearly have loved to include. For that reason, I do not see ‘Matereality V2’ as a definitive survey. It is more a bird’s-eye view of what I have been noticing over the past few years – a snapshot of emerging and established artists finding inventive ways to make material inseparable from meaning. The process also became very visual. I had images of the works with me and, over time, I found myself linking particular works together. Sometimes those connections were material, but often they were conceptual, emotional or contradictory.

For example, I began thinking about Warren Maroon’s work in relation to Senzeni Marasela’s because both opened up complicated ideas around home – home as a place of comfort, intimacy and belonging, but also of pain, absence or difficulty. I also realised that placing Sepideh Mehraban’s work alongside Ben Stanwix and Xhanti Zwelendaba’s BAWA work created an interesting conversation around place and printing. In different ways, both use imprinting and reproduction to think about how place is recorded, remembered and mediated. From there, Mehraban’s work connected very strongly to Tamlin Blake’s. Mehraban’s carpet carries newspaper imprints, while Blake works directly with newspaper and references book burning. Both bring to mind the ways authoritarian societies can limit access to knowledge and, in doing so, restrict individual autonomy. The newspaper becomes more than a material or source image; it carries questions of information, censorship, power and who is allowed access to knowledge. Gaelen Pinnock’s work began speaking to Lungisa Qwanta’s in ways that became clearer the longer I lived with the images.

Other pairings came almost instinctively. I could not resist placing Yonela Makoba’s teabag work in conversation with Zaneaca Singh’s sugar works. Tea and sugar are so intimately linked to comfort, hospitality and everyday ritual, yet both are deeply entangled with colonial trade, extraction and systems whose consequences continue to be felt today. Atang Tshikare and Lyndi Sales were another pairing that became exciting to me. Their works open onto connections between cosmology, science, plants, natural systems and forms of knowledge that move between the earthly and the speculative. I placed the work of Chris Soal in conversation with Hanien Conradie’s work. Soal found the bottle caps he uses in the streets of Johannesburg, while Conradie gathered her materials from riverbanks and plants. I was interested in that contrast between the inorganic and the organic – two artists collecting from their immediate environments but encountering very different traces of place. One gathers the discarded remnants of an urban and consumer landscape; the other works with materials embedded in natural systems. I also put Sahlah Davids and Jeanne Gaigher in the same room. Both had been working abstractly and, for works made specifically for this exhibition, began experimenting with figuration. I loved that parallel: two artists independently shifting their visual languages and then finding themselves in conversation within the exhibition.

There are many more connections, and they became central to the curatorial process. One work would lead me to another, sometimes through material, sometimes through process, and sometimes through a shared political or emotional concern. The exhibition gradually became a web of relationships rather than a series of isolated objects. At one stage I considered making the exhibition entirely South African. There was certainly enough work to do that. But ultimately, it felt too restrictive, partly because of the political moment we are living through, when xenophobia and increasingly narrow ideas about nationality and belonging remain so present, but also because this kind of material experimentation is something I have noticed strongly across the African continent.

The final selection was never simply about finding unusual materials. I was interested in artists for whom material is fundamental to the meaning of the work – where you could not simply substitute one material for another without changing what the artwork is saying. That is also why I am drawn to thematic exhibitions. They allow artists across race, gender, age, generation, geography, medium and levels of recognition to enter into a shared conversation. Their differences are not erased, but neither are they confined to fixed categories. Instead, the question becomes: what might very different artists contribute to the same conversation? I am always interested in creating encounters between works that might otherwise never occupy the same room. At the same time, I do not want to explain every connection. Some relationships are quite deliberate, and others emerged unexpectedly, and I hope audiences discover many of them for themselves. A viewer may make a connection that I did not anticipate at all, and that is part of what makes an exhibition alive. blocks.text: Material can carry histories of place, labour, culture and exchange. How does the exhibition explore meaning gathered through use, movement and transformation?

Many of the materials in ‘Matereality V2’ have already had lives before they enter the museum. They have circulated through homes, industries, communities, ceremonies, economies or systems of trade and consumption. Through cutting, stitching, weaving, assembling, burning, layering, binding or repetition, those meanings can shift again. Something disposable can become precious. An ordinary domestic material can become political. An industrial product can suddenly speak about the body, land, memory or belonging. As the exhibition developed, I found myself returning to Jane Bennett’s idea of “vibrant matter”. Bennett asks us to reconsider the assumption that matter is passive – that human beings act upon materials and materials obediently receive that action. Instead, she encourages us to think of materials as having their own properties, behaviours and capacities. That became very useful to me while thinking through ‘Matereality’, because artists do not always completely control their materials. Materials sag, crack, stretch, absorb, rust, decay, reflect and resist. Sometimes the artist is working with the material rather than simply imposing something upon it. So you cannot really separate material, process and meaning in many of these works. Very often, the material itself helps to produce that meaning. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

blocks.text: What role does experimentation play in the exhibition, especially in how artists encounter, manipulate or reconsider their materials?

Experimentation is everything. I am constantly fascinated by the ability of artists to look at a material that most of us might overlook and imagine an entirely different function, language or aesthetic for it. There is often an enormous amount of testing, intuition and problem-solving involved: discovering how far something will stretch, what happens when it is heated, cut, stitched, compressed, layered, woven or combined with another material. Sometimes the material refuses to behave as the artist imagined. That resistance is important. There can be a negotiation between artist and material. Materials have characteristics and limitations of their own. They can buckle, unravel, stain, rust, fade, harden, break down or change over time. I think that curiosity is one of the great pleasures of ‘Materiality ’. The exhibition repeatedly asks a very simple question: what else can this thing become? And very often the answer is something completely unexpected. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

blocks.caption: Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

blocks.text: How does ‘Matereality V2’ invite audiences to think about the relationship between an artwork’s physical qualities and the ideas or experiences it communicates?

I hope people first encounter the works physically. Before reading a wall text or knowing the story, there is texture, scale, weight, fragility, repetition, colour, density and surface. You might immediately wonder what something is made from, how it was constructed, or even what it might feel like to touch. Then, when you understand why that particular material has been used, the artwork can shift completely. A material that initially appears seductive might carry a difficult history. Something apparently cheap or disposable might involve extraordinary labour. Something visually delicate may come from an industrial or violent process. That relationship between the sensory and the conceptual is central to the exhibition. Sometimes the conversation between two works only becomes apparent when you stand between them. A material used in one work might change the way you understand another. A shared concern with home, violence, memory, science, comfort or colonial history may surface even where the artists are working in completely different ways. For me, that is one of the pleasures of a thematic exhibition. Meaning does not only exist within individual works; it can also happen in the space between them. And I hope viewers find links that I have missed entirely. I also think this physical encounter has particular resonance now. So much of our experience of art – and of the world generally – happens through screens. We scroll past images incredibly quickly. These works ask for another kind of attention. The exhibition asks us not only to look at what an artwork represents, but to consider what it is physically made from, what that material has already experienced, and what the artist has asked it to become. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

blocks.text: The exhibition brings different artistic approaches into conversation within a museum context. How did Iziko’s spaces and collections shape your curatorial thinking?

Working within Iziko inevitably means thinking about history, because the museum contains layers of collecting, classification and ideas about what kinds of artworks and materials have historically been considered worthy of entering a national collection. That becomes particularly interesting with an exhibition such as ‘Matereality’, because many of the artists work with practices or materials historically associated with craft, domestic labour, informal economies or everyday life rather than so-called “fine art”. This second iteration places a stronger emphasis on textile practices, Afro-centric perspectives and indigenous knowledge systems. I am particularly interested in the way practices such as weaving, stitching, beadwork and other forms of hand-making hold knowledge. Historically, many of these practices were separated from “fine art” and placed into categories such as craft, decoration or domestic production. But they contain sophisticated systems of knowledge, memory and transmission. Many contemporary artists are actively drawing upon, disrupting or transforming those traditions. This connects to why thematic exhibitions are so useful within a museum context. I can only speak from my own position as a curator, and I would never claim that an individual exhibition can resolve the much larger structural contradictions within museums or art history. But exhibitions remain one of the most immediate and practical tools available to me. They allow me to work across some of the divisions through which art history and museum collections have traditionally been organised.

There is also a practical institutional reality behind this. When budgets and procedures for growing collections are very limited, exhibitions become another way of bringing artistic voices into the museum, even when we are not yet in a position to acquire those works. They allow us to broaden the conversation, introduce artists who may be absent from the permanent collection and test new relationships between historical holdings and contemporary practice. There is another contradiction that ‘Matereality’ brings into focus too. Museums are designed to preserve things. We try to prevent objects from changing. But many contemporary artists deliberately work with materials that change. They fade. Rust. Break down. Become brittle. Decay. So these works raise fascinating questions about what a museum actually preserves. Is it the original material? The artist’s intention? The process? Can components eventually be replaced? At what point does replacing something fundamentally alter the artwork? That tension is increasingly important for contemporary collections: the museum seeks permanence, while matter itself is often impermanent.
How do questions of place and contemporary life in South Africa enter the exhibition through the artists’ materials, processes and perspectives?

They enter organically because materials are deeply connected to place. Artists work with what surrounds them – culturally, economically, environmentally and politically. Within South Africa, materials can carry extraordinarily complicated histories. They can speak about mining and extraction, land and displacement, migrant labour, clothing and identity, domestic work, inequality, environmental degradation, spirituality, indigenous knowledge systems and histories of making. But I did not want those themes to become neat categories. I did not want textiles in one room, plastic in another and found objects somewhere else. The interesting part is precisely how these histories and materials become entangled. At the same time, I did not want the exhibition to imply that South African artists are somehow only responding to South African concerns. These practices are connected to much larger questions around climate change, consumption, migration, technology, sustainability and belonging. That is one reason the exhibition extends beyond South Africa to selected artists elsewhere on the continent. There is extraordinary material experimentation happening across Africa, often using objects or substances that are locally specific while simultaneously speaking to global systems and concerns. What interests me is precisely that movement between the local and the universal. A material might have a highly specific social history in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Accra, or Harare, but the artwork can simultaneously open onto a much broader conversation about contemporary life. blocks.text: What questions do you hope ‘Matereality V2’ leaves open about the materials around us and how we understand their histories, possibilities and value?

I hope people leave the exhibition looking at ordinary materials differently. We live surrounded by objects and substances whose histories we rarely think about: where they came from, who made them, what labour was involved, what systems of trade or extraction produced them, what environmental cost they carry, and where they will eventually end up. Artists are particularly good at disrupting that familiarity. They can take something we think we understand and make it strange again. Questions of value are crucial here. Why is one material considered precious and another disposable? Why are certain forms of making described as art while others have historically been classified as craft, domestic labour or decoration? Who decides what is worthy of preservation? I also hope people leave thinking about the relationships between the works. I have spent years carrying these images around, mentally and quite literally, and gradually seeing connections between artists who may never have imagined themselves alongside one another. But once the exhibition opens, those relationships no longer belong only to me. A visitor may see an entirely different connection between two works – through a material, a memory, a colour, a history or an experience. I like the idea that the exhibition can keep generating conversations beyond the ones I consciously constructed. So perhaps it leaves visitors with fairly simple questions: what histories are contained within the objects we encounter every day? Whose labour is embedded within them? Why do we value some things and discard others? What happens when the same material can signify comfort and violence, familiarity and exploitation, intimacy and enormous global systems at the same time? And what possibilities might exist in a material once we stop seeing it only in terms of its intended function? Of course, exhibitions centred on materiality are incredibly common, and artists have been investigating material for centuries. I am certainly not suggesting that ‘Matereality’ introduces something entirely new. My hope is rather to pull together some of the many threads running through contemporary practice – labour, ecology, indigenous knowledge, craft, memory, technology, consumption and value – and see what becomes visible when they are considered together.

In that sense, ‘Matereality V2’ is perhaps an opportunity to take stock: a kind of summary of what I have been noticing over the past several years, and of the extraordinarily inventive ways in which emerging and established artists are making material inseparable from meaning. What I hope it offers is another chapter in that much longer conversation. And perhaps it encourages us to pay closer attention to the things around us – to what materials already contain, to the labour and histories embedded within them, and to what happens when an artist takes something familiar and allows us to see it completely differently.
This exhibition is on view at the Iziko South African National Gallery in Cape Town until 30th June 2027.
